Chapter 6. The Reckoning—Learning to Stay with Discomfort
There’s this quiet, easily missed moment that follows right after the shock of a setback.
You know that urge to escape, to distract yourself, or just to numb out? That’s when it hits hardest. Most of us don’t even realize how quickly we reach for our phones, pour another drink, or throw ourselves into work... all just to avoid that uncomfortable feeling simmering underneath.
Picture a young designer who’s just gotten some tough feedback on a project she poured her heart into. The sting of that criticism is still fresh, so she finds herself scrolling endlessly through social media. Sure, the feed offers a quick escape, but as the hours slip by, that discomfort doesn’t fade—it actually grows heavier, more tangled.
Eventually, she realizes the only way out... is through. Late at night, she finally lets herself sit with the ache. She notices the tightness in her chest, the heat rising in her face, the swirl of anxious thoughts. It’s uncomfortable—maybe even painful—but it’s real.
And here’s something most people miss: it takes so much energy to keep dodging these feelings. Yet, when you simply acknowledge them, things can feel unexpectedly lighter.
Now, staying with discomfort isn’t about wallowing or beating yourself up. It’s about letting your emotions have space—to be felt, without judgment or rush.
Think of a parent, after a heated argument with their partner. Instead of storming out or shutting down, he sits quietly, breathing through the tension, letting the anger and sadness move through him. And in that stillness, he discovers a sliver of clarity—a sense that, yes, these feelings are intense... but they’re also temporary.
So many of us fall into the trap of thinking that discomfort means we’ve failed—or that we’re just not strong enough. But here’s the truth: discomfort is actually a sign of growth. It’s your mind and body’s way of saying, “Hey, something important is happening here.”
By choosing to stay present, even just for a moment, you give yourself the chance to learn from the experience, instead of letting it take the wheel.
For example, a teacher overwhelmed by a new curriculum notices her urge to vent or distract herself with busywork. One afternoon, she decides to close her classroom door and just sit quietly. She lets the frustration and fear wash over her, paying attention to the stories in her mind. And in that pause, she realizes—she’s not alone. Chances are, many of her colleagues feel exactly the same way.
The reckoning? It’s not a one-time event. It’s a practice—a choice you make each time discomfort shows up. Every time you stay, notice, and learn, you’re building emotional resilience.
And that’s how you start facing life’s challenges with a little more courage, and a whole lot more clarity.
